title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service allegedly recorded virtual meetings without obtaining consent from all participants, then used those recordings to train its AI system. The service operated at scale, processing over 1 billion meetings across millions of users. The deployment failure was in the default settings and consent mechanism, where the system recorded by default rather than requiring affirmative permission from meeting participants before recording began.

The lawsuit alleges that the company's stated consent process, a checkbox in its privacy policy, did not reliably prevent recording of users who had not agreed to participate. Social media complaints describe the service joining meetings and recording automatically. It is not established whether the company's de-identification process was effective, whether users were systematically deceived, or what the court will ultimately find.

This incident would have been caught by requiring affirmative opt-in consent from all meeting participants before recording began, and by auditing whether the stated consent mechanism actually prevented recording in cases where participants had not agreed.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed Friday accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence transcription company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California, alleges that Otter's transcription service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without asking all participants for consent. The company then allegedly uses these recordings to train its AI systems for financial gain, violating state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. Otter has approximately 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since its 2016 founding.

Otter's privacy policy states it obtains explicit permission through a checkbox allowing the company to use meeting transcripts for training purposes, but the lawsuit contends many users are still being deceived. Recent complaints on social media platforms describe the service joining meetings automatically and recording conversations without consent. While Otter claims it de-identifies audio data before using it for machine learning, the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information and guarantees speaker anonymity. Neither Brewer's legal team nor Otter responded to requests for comment.
